title: Video Killed The Radio Star
description: The synth-pop prophecy that launched MTV as its very first video.

pops.text: Pop-up prophecy! This 1979 single literally predicted the video age — two years before MTV even existed.
Trevor Horn, Geoff Downes and Bruce Woolley wrote this in 1978, inspired in part by a J.G. Ballard story about a singer made obsolete by technology.
It wasn't even first by The Buggles — co-writer Bruce Woolley released his own version months earlier with his band The Camera Club, featuring a young Thomas Dolby.
Chart split! This hit No. 1 in the UK and 15 other countries, but only reached No. 40 in America — until television changed everything.
Spot the future Oscar winner! That's a 22-year-old Hans Zimmer in the black jacket miming keyboards — decades before The Lion King and Dune.
Director Russell Mulcahy shot this in south London in just one day, on a then-huge $50,000 budget. He'd go on to define the early MTV look.
At 12:01 a.m. on August 1, 1981, this became the first music video ever played on MTV. You couldn't pick a more fitting first word.
It was also Island Records' first UK No. 1 single — and Horn and Downes were briefly poached to join prog legends Yes.
Full circle: MTV later marked this as its millionth video aired, and it was also the first video shown on MTV Classic in the UK in 2010.

title: Love Will Tear Us Apart
description: Joy Division's haunting signature single — joyful title flipped, heartbreakingly, on its head.

pops.text: That title is a joke with a sting — a deliberate flip of Captain & Tennille's sunny hit 'Love Will Keep Us Together.'
Written in August–September 1979, the lyrics reflected Ian Curtis's crumbling marriage and his struggles after being diagnosed with epilepsy that year.
Rare sight: this is one of the few Joy Division songs where Curtis plays guitar — his bandmates taught him to strum a D chord for it.
They recorded it twice. Curtis and producer Martin Hannett disliked the January 1980 Pennine Studios take, so they re-cut it at Strawberry Studios with a more crooning vocal.
The band filmed this video themselves on April 28, 1980, rehearsing at T.J. Davidson's studio — an old haunt from their earliest days.
DIY to the end: the colour 'browns out' in places, and the sound recorded on the day was so poor the label swapped in the single version, wrecking the lip-sync.
This was Joy Division's only promotional video. Curtis died less than three weeks after filming it, aged just 23.
Released as a standalone single, it became their first chart hit — No. 13 in the UK — and later topped the chart in New Zealand.
NME named this the greatest single of all time in 2002. Its title is now Curtis's epitaph, inscribed on his memorial stone by his widow Deborah.

title: Jessie's Girl
description: A stained-glass class crush turned into the ultimate song about wanting your friend's girlfriend.

pops.text: True story! Springfield fell for a classmate's girlfriend in a stained-glass class in Pasadena in the late 1970s — and never even learned her name.
The friend wasn't Jessie — he was Gary. 'Gary's Girl' didn't sing well, 'Randy's Girl' almost stuck, then a Ron Jessie football shirt settled it.
That's not Springfield on those crunching guitars — Pat Benatar's guitarist (and husband) Neil Giraldo played both guitar and bass on the track.
Producer Keith Olsen, of Fleetwood Mac fame, helmed the Working Class Dog album — named for Springfield's dog Ronnie, who poses on the cover.
In the video, 'Jessie' — played by actor Steve Antin — spray-paints the song's title on a brick wall while Springfield watches the couple walk off.
That bathroom mirror smash? It reportedly took 24 takes — and 24 mirrors — to get right.
Slow burn: the single took 19 weeks to climb to No. 1, finally topping the Billboard Hot 100 for two weeks.
Perfect timing — it was the No. 1 song in America the week MTV launched, August 1, 1981, while Springfield was also starring as Dr. Noah Drake on General Hospital.
It won Springfield the 1982 Grammy for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance. And the real Jessie's Girl? Oprah's team tried to find her and failed — she likely never knew.

title: I Ran (So Far Away)
description: Alien abduction, auroras and the most famous haircut of the 1980s, beamed in from Liverpool.

pops.text: Singer Mike Score was a Liverpool hairdresser who rehearsed above his own salon — which explains a lot about what you're about to see on his head.
Two sparks made this song: a band at Liverpool's Eric's Club with a tune called 'I Ran,' and a poster at Zoo Records of a couple fleeing a flying saucer.
So yes, it's a sci-fi song — a man spots a girl beneath an aurora, panics, runs, and the pair get swept up by aliens.
Three sizes fit all: the album version runs 5:07, this video version 3:58, and the radio edit 3:43.
That foil-covered room is a tribute to Brian Eno and Robert Fripp's '(No Pussyfooting)' album cover — and you can spot the cameras reflected in the floor mirrors.
Director Tony van den Ende's cheap clip got hammered on early MTV in summer 1982 — and American success followed.
Chart paradox: No. 1 in Australia and No. 9 in the US, but only No. 43 in their native UK.
The band were no joke to Grammy voters — their instrumental 'D.N.A.' from the same album won Best Rock Instrumental Performance in 1983.
That haircut became shorthand for the whole decade — name-checked in Pulp Fiction and The Wedding Singer, and revived for a new generation in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.

title: Your Love
description: Josie's on vacation — and this 20-minute songwriting sprint became an eternal sing-along.

pops.text: Written in about 20 minutes! Guitarist John Spinks penned it at his East London flat, with singer Tony Lewis perched on an amplifier beside him.
Confession time: there's no real Josie. Spinks confirmed the whole cheating-while-she's-on-vacation story is completely invented.
Listen to Lewis's soaring tenor — he shaped his vocal approach with Sting of The Police firmly in mind.
Producer William Wittman pushed the band from a softer demo toward a harder sound, taking cues from The Who and The Police.
Baseball-crazy name, zero baseball: the London trio first called themselves The Baseball Boys, after a gang in the film The Warriors.
Director Jon Jopson's video is a video-within-a-video — the band perform in front of the Play Deep album cover while an artist finger-paints it offstage.
The painter is actress JoAnn Willette, later of TV's Just the Ten of Us. The clip peaked at No. 2 on MTV's Top 20 Countdown in April 1986.
It reached No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100 and powered debut album Play Deep to No. 9 and triple-platinum sales in the US — while stalling at No. 83 back home in the UK.
The ultimate slow burn: in March 2026, this video passed one billion views on YouTube — 40 years after release.

title: She Drives Me Crazy
description: A falsetto, a ruler-whacked snare, and a session inside Prince's Paisley Park produced the Cannibals' transatlantic No. 1.

pops.text: This arrived in the studio with a different name — it started life titled 'She's My Baby' before becoming 'She Drives Me Crazy.'
It was recorded in Studio B at Paisley Park, Prince's Minnesota complex — lava lamps, Prince's gear, and all.
The band dreamed of Prince producing them. He didn't produce for hire, so they got his associate David Z instead — Prince's right-hand studio man.
That famous snare 'pop'? David Z whacked a loose snare skin with a wooden ruler, EQ'd it hard around 1kHz, and blended it with a Linn 9000 sample.
He then replayed that sound through a small speaker sitting upside-down on another snare drum, so the real snares rattled underneath for extra fizz.
The song only clicked when Roland Gift flipped the verses into falsetto — that high, twitchy vocal became its signature alongside the snare.
Guitarist Andy Cox played the riff on Prince's Rickenbacker, and the band ran keyboards through Prince's wah-wah pedals while they were there.
Chart takeover: No. 5 in the UK — the band's biggest home hit — and No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on April 15, 1989.
Two videos were made. Philippe Decouflé's surreal dancer version scored 4 nominations at the 1989 MTV VMAs, including Video of the Year.

title: Bust A Move
description: Written in 90 minutes in a USC apartment, this Flea-powered party rap became hip-hop's friendliest Grammy winner.

pops.text: Young MC — real name Marvin Young — wrote these lyrics in about 90 minutes in his USC campus apartment. First draft, never edited.
He was Delicious Vinyl's secret weapon: before his own hit, he co-wrote Tone Lōc's smash 'Wild Thing.'
The whole groove is built on a sample of 'Found a Child' by Ballin' Jack — that bassline loop never lets up.
Sample collage alert: the breakdown stitches in Dennis Coffey's 'Scorpio' and Bette Midler's 'Daytime Hustler,' with LinnDrum hits from RoyalCash.
Spot the bass player: that's Flea from Red Hot Chili Peppers on bass — and in the video, in his famous stuffed-animal pants.
That huge chorus hook is Crystal Blake, a Stevie Wonder backing singer — despite rumors at the time that it was Diana Ross.
Why isn't he dancing? The video casts Young MC as a Rod Serling-style narrator, Twilight Zone-style, describing the action behind him — label boss Mike Ross's idea.
Director Tamra Davis shot the ultra-literal video — every lyric gets acted out. Davis later directed Billy Madison and Half Baked.
It peaked at No. 7 in the US, No. 1 in Australia, went platinum, hung around the Hot 100 for 39 weeks — and won the 1990 Grammy for Best Rap Performance.

title: Groove Is in the Heart
description: A Herbie Hancock loop, Bootsy, Q-Tip and a slide whistle collided in NYC clubs to create the happiest dance record of 1990.

pops.text: Deee-Lite were a true world clique: Lady Miss Kier from Ohio, DJ Dmitry from Ukraine, and Towa Tei from Japan, formed on New York's club scene.
They'd written this in the late '80s and were already performing it live in 1989, a year before the album version was recorded.
That unstoppable riff is a loop of Herbie Hancock's 'Bring Down the Birds,' from the 1966 Blow-Up soundtrack — Hancock got a writing credit.
The drums and that bonkers slide-whistle breakdown come from Vernon Burch's 'Get Up.' Yes, a slide whistle is the secret weapon.
Hear that stuttered 'I, I-I-I-I'? It's a sample of Eva Gabor on the Green Acres theme saying 'I get allergic smelling hay.'
Kier wrote the lyrics before she even heard the loop — and in 1988 she mailed Bootsy Collins a fan letter with their demo. He called back.
Bootsy brought the P-Funk family with him: Maceo Parker on sax and Fred Wesley on trombone — James Brown's Horny Horns, on a house record.
Q-Tip dropped by the studio, heard the track, asked for 15 minutes to write — and came back with that perfect guest rap.
No. 1 in Australia and on the US dance chart, No. 2 in the UK, No. 4 in the US. Hiroyuki Nakano's psychedelic video was nominated at the 1991 MTV VMAs.

title: Enjoy the Silence
description: A funereal harmonium ballad sped up into Depeche Mode's biggest-ever single — and Dave Gahan crowned king of emptiness.

pops.text: Martin Gore's original demo was nothing like this — just him singing slowly over a harmonium, a quiet ballad in C minor.
Alan Wilder heard the line 'All I ever wanted' and heard it in Neil Tennant of the Pet Shop Boys' voice — he knew it wanted a pulse.
Wilder and producer Flood rebuilt it up-tempo in secret. Gore hated the idea at first — a song called 'Enjoy the Silence' was supposed to be serene.
Then Gore walked in, played that icy guitar riff over the new backing, Gahan sang it — and the band knew instantly. It was the one time in the studio they knew they had a hit.
Released February 5, 1990 as the second single from Violator, following 'Personal Jesus.'
Director Anton Corbijn took inspiration from The Little Prince: a king who has everything, wandering the world with a deckchair, looking for somewhere to just sit.
Filming took Gahan to Balmoral in Scotland, the Algarve in Portugal, and the Swiss Alps. He later admitted dragging the cape through snow made him feel 'like an idiot.'
Fed up with the cold in the Alps, Gahan handed the crown and robe to producer Richard Bell and left by helicopter — the distant snow shots at the end are Bell, not Dave.
No. 6 in the UK, No. 8 in the US — still Depeche Mode's highest-charting US single — their best-selling single ever, and winner of Best British Single at the 1991 BRIT Awards.

title: Torn
description: The fourth recording of a lost L.A. song became the biggest airplay hit in the world — without ever being sold as a US single.

pops.text: Natalie didn't write this — Scott Cutler, Anne Preven and Phil Thornalley wrote it in 1991 as a solo song for Preven.
The first recording wasn't in English at all: Danish singer Lis Sørensen released it as 'Brændt' in 1993.
The writers' own band Ednaswap released a much heavier rock version in 1995, and Trine Rein covered it in 1996 — Imbruglia's was the fourth version.
Imbruglia was an ex-soap star — Beth Brennan on Neighbours — whose demo of 'Torn' won her the RCA deal. Co-writer Thornalley produced her version.
Her version was recorded in Kilburn, London, and mixed by Nigel Godrich — who that same era was shaping Radiohead's sound.
Director Alison Maclean shot the video as one locked-off take of an apartment. The boyfriend is British actor Jeremy Sheffield.
The twist: they're rehearsing a scene Maclean adapted from Last Tango in Paris, while the director and crew keep walking in to reset them.

At the end the crew literally dismantles the apartment around her — it was a soundstage all along. She later said she wore baggy army pants because she was deeply insecure and refused to wear a dress.

The chart paradox: No. 1 on US airplay for 11 weeks, No. 2 in the UK, over 4 million sold, a Grammy nomination — but only No. 42 on the Hot 100, because Billboard barred songs with no US physical single, and her label withheld one to sell the album.

title: Tubthumping
description: An anarchist collective walks into a Leeds pub and walks out with the most unstoppable get-up-again chant of the 90s.

pops.text: That stern spoken intro is lifted straight from the British miners film Brassed Off. The album version opens with Pete Postlethwaite in full brass-band defiance mode.
Chumbawamba were not a pop band — they were an anarchist collective formed in Burnley in 1982. This was their eighth album and their first for a major label, EMI.
The song was inspired by nights at the Fforde Grene pub in Leeds. Guitarist Boff Whalley has said it is really about the resilience of ordinary working-class people.
Listen to Jude Abbott's trumpet solo — she sneaks in Jeremiah Clarke's Trumpet Voluntary from around 1700. A Baroque fanfare hiding inside a drinking anthem.
The video, directed by Ben Unwin, is set in a pub with the punters frozen in place. The band performs on a tiny TV in the corner before spilling out into the bar itself.
It spent three weeks at No. 2 in the UK, stuck behind Will Smith's Men in Black. It still sold 880,000 copies in Britain alone.
In America it peaked at No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100 but ruled the airwaves — No. 1 on Hot 100 Airplay for nine weeks, plus No. 1 on three other Billboard charts.

At the 1998 BRIT Awards, where it was nominated for Best British Single, singer Danbert Nobacon poured a bucket of water over Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott in support of striking Liverpool dockers.
Gamers know it from EA's World Cup 98 soundtrack, which helped turn a pub chant into a global sports anthem. I get knocked down, indeed.

title: Fly Away
description: The hit Lenny almost left off the album became his first UK No. 1 and launched a record four-year Grammy streak.

pops.text: This song nearly never made the album. Kravitz had already finished and handed in 5 when he cut Fly Away, and first thought of it as a B-side.
A friend heard the tape and insisted it was a hit. Kravitz called Virgin back and the label reluctantly squeezed it onto the finished album at the last minute.
It grew out of goofing around testing a new amplifier in the Bahamas at Compass Point Studios. Four simple chords, one monster riff, done.
It was only the fourth single from 5, released in 1998. Nobody — including the label — initially clocked that the last-minute add-on would be the big one.
Director Paul Hunter shot the video as a sweaty club gig, with the band playing to a dancing, making-out crowd. Effects were added to make the footage look deliberately beat-up and worn.
In the US it peaked at No. 12 on the Hot 100 but topped both the Mainstream Rock and Modern Rock charts. Radio could not leave it alone.
Britain went bigger: it hit No. 1 in February 1999, selling over 123,000 copies in its first week and knocking Blondie's comeback hit Maria off the top.
Its UK surge got a big assist from TV — the song soundtracked a Peugeot 206 car commercial that put the riff in every living room in the country.
Fly Away won the 1999 Grammy for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance. It was the first of four straight wins for Kravitz in that category, a record streak through 2002.

title: Dog Days Are Over
description: A title spotted from a bicycle, recorded by banging on studio walls, that exploded two years later on live TV.

pops.text: Florence Welch got the title from a giant rainbow text artwork by Ugo Rondinone on London's South Bank. She rode past it on her bike over Waterloo Bridge every day.
Dog days refers to the dog star, Sirius, and the sluggish heat of late summer. When Sirius moves away, everyone wakes up — that release is the whole song.
It was recorded with no instruments in a Crystal Palace studio Welch described as the size of a loo. The pounding drums? That is the band banging on the studio walls.
Welch co-wrote it with Isabella Summers, the Machine herself, who plays piano on it. Producer James Ford, of Simian Mobile Disco, produced and mixed the track.
That glittering harp is Tom Monger, and the handclaps and stomps build the song like a gospel revival. It was Florence's second single, first released 1 December 2008.

First time around it only reached No. 89 in the UK. This is actually the second video — a polished 2010 re-release directed by Georgie Greville and Geremy Jasper, with dancers, drummers and a gospel choir.
The first video could not have been cheaper: shot on one camera in Sydenham Woods, with Welch's dad dressed as a clown. The 2010 video won Best Art Direction at the MTV VMAs.
Her live VMA performance in September 2010 changed everything in America — downloads jumped 257% in a week and the song leapt to No. 21 on the Billboard Hot 100, her first US Top 30 hit.
Fifteen years on, it soundtracks the finale of Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 in 2023 and hit its biggest Spotify streaming day ever, peaking at a new UK high of No. 21.

title: Happy
description: Written for Gru falling in love, first recorded by someone else, then turned into the world's first 24-hour music video.

pops.text: Pharrell wrote this for Despicable Me 2, for the moment reformed villain Gru falls in love and dances down the street. Pure joy was the assignment.
It was not meant to be a Pharrell single at all — he wrote it for CeeLo Green, who recorded his own version. Pharrell has said he thinks CeeLo's version is better.
CeeLo's label shelved his recording because his Christmas album was coming out. So the song came back to Pharrell, and became the lead single from his album G I R L.
This four-minute clip is the edit of a genuine first: the world's first 24-hour music video, launched at 24hoursofhappy.com and directed by French duo We Are From L.A.
The long version loops the song with over 400 different people dancing through Los Angeles, shot on Steadicam. The crew walked about eight miles a day for 11 days.
Spot the cameos in the full cut: Steve Carell, Jamie Foxx, Jimmy Kimmel and Magic Johnson all show up — and Pharrell himself appears 24 times, once at the top of every hour.
It held No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for 10 consecutive weeks and topped charts in more than 20 countries. In the UK it hit No. 1 on three separate occasions, a record at the time.
It finished as the best-selling song of 2014 in both the US, with 6.45 million copies that year, and the UK, with 1.5 million. Billboard also named it the No. 1 single of 2014.
It was Oscar-nominated for Best Original Song, losing to Let It Go, but won two Grammys in 2015: Best Pop Solo Performance for a live version, and Best Music Video.

title: Feel It Still
description: An Alaskan psych-rock band borrows a 1961 Motown melody, writes a hit in 45 minutes, and wins a Grammy.

pops.text: That melody is not an accident — it openly borrows from the Marvelettes' 1961 Motown classic Please Mr. Postman. The original writers are credited, including Motown legend Brian Holland.
Portugal. The Man formed in Wasilla, Alaska, and this was album number eight. After 14 years of cult psych-rock, this 2-minute-43-second pop song was their first ever Hot 100 entry.
Bassist Zach Carothers has joked about how fast it came together: they wrote it in about 45 minutes in the studio. And then, in his words, it won them a Grammy.

The album Woodstock got its name and spark from frontman John Gourley's dad showing him his original ticket stub from the 1969 Woodstock festival. The band scrapped a nearly finished album, Gloomin + Doomin, to make it instead.

The video has Gourley dancing through a junkyard in white overalls while a man torches a newspaper labelled Info Wars. An interactive version hid 30 clickable resistance tools and causes as Easter eggs.
It was a true sleeper hit — released in March 2017, it took eight months to peak at No. 4 on the Hot 100 in November. Word of mouth and playlists did the work.
On alternative radio it was a monster: 20 weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's Alternative Songs chart, breaking the record Muse's Madness had held at 19 weeks.
It eventually topped six different Billboard airplay charts at once — a crossover feat no act had managed since Gotye's Somebody That I Used to Know in 2012.
In January 2018 it won Best Pop Duo/Group Performance at the Grammys, beating Coldplay and The Chainsmokers. It has since been certified 7x Platinum in the US.
